signals.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
signals.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. signals.title: Out There
signals.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! BECOME A SUPPORTER Do you believe in this newsletter’s mission — to help us all stay human and engaged and creative in a world of (mis)information overload and AI distraction? Then you should join the community of TAoN Supporters! You’ll get access to the full archives as well as Supporter-only bonus posts and threads. Your support makes this newsletter possible. Seriously. Thank you! Subscribe now THE NEXT FREE EDITION IN TWO WEEKS! IN OTHER NEWS David Lee Roth , EMT . “ Reading Maps plots the routes characters travel in novels and films — you can trace the Pequod’s ocean path as it chases Moby Dick, or Victor Frankenstein’s pursuit of his monster from Geneva to the Arctic.” — Recomendo Lighthouses of the World , a digital map. Via Popular Science . “What Gertrude Stein, T. S. Eliot and Joan Didion Really Meant With Their Most Famous Aphorisms .” The International Dada Archive collects scanned Dada pamphlets from the early 20th century. Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. More from Mark here . Shadows . Via Street Art Utopia. Tobie Tse “combines hand-stitched textiles, illustration and digital motion to create visual responses to music.” Tom Waits spoken word piece : OKAY THAT’S IT! Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. visualFeast.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
visualFeast.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. Website ⌘ Github Thanks for reading. — Bora / Nirmata Studio

visualFeast.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! IN OTHER NEWS David Lee Roth , EMT . “ Reading Maps plots the routes characters travel in novels and films — you can trace the Pequod’s ocean path as it chases Moby Dick, or Victor Frankenstein’s pursuit of his monster from Geneva to the Arctic.” — Recomendo Lighthouses of the World , a digital map. Via Popular Science . “What Gertrude Stein, T. S. Eliot and Joan Didion Really Meant With Their Most Famous Aphorisms .” The International Dada Archive collects scanned Dada pamphlets from the early 20th century. Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. More from Mark here . Shadows . Via Street Art Utopia. visualFeast.title: Step by step: How to find Design System + AI jobs faster with Claude Code and MCP
visualFeast.description: I gave our Design System job board an MCP server. Your AI agent can read the whole job board now. (What is an MCP? MCP is the standard that lets an agent call a tool instead of scraping a web page) Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Why? Good roles go early. By the time you have scrolled the job board and opened twelve tabs and read the postings properly the pile on the recruiter’s desk is deep. There are 225 open Design System roles on the board right now. Every one of them is checked by hand and closed postings drop out. Nobody reads 225 postings. You read four and apply to two. Your agent works through all of them. It runs at https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp It needs no key and no account and it can only read Below are the 30 prompts I run against it The last ones hand the whole job over to a cron job that checks the board every morning for you What is inside One line to connect the server. Everything after it is a prompt. 23 prompts for finding roles and reading salary bands and closing skill gaps and preparing for the interview. 7 prompts that hand the search to a cron job so your Mac checks the board while you sleep. The five tools and what each one answers. Step 1: connect it One line in your terminal (1 min) Paste this in Claude Code: claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp The -s user part registers it for every folder. Leave it out and the server only exists in the folder you happened to be in. Then restart Claude Code once because tools load when a session starts. Quit it with /exit and start it again and ask “which tools do you have from ids-jobs?” No terminal at all? Claude Desktop and claude.ai do it in the interface: Settings then Connectors then Add custom connector. Paste the URL and start a new chat. Cursor and every other MCP client work too. The setup page has the config for each of them. Step 2: the prompts Put your CV in the folder you start Claude Code in or simply describe your skills. Then use these. Every number under a prompt is what the board answered on 21 August 2026. I want the roles that are worth my time Five prompts that cut 225 postings down to the handful you would actually take. 1. “Which Design System roles were posted in the last two weeks? Optional: Which of them fit my CV?” The one I use most. 57 roles came in over the last fourteen days. Here are the five newest: Malt Head of Experience Systems & AI France / Germany 21 Aug ICEYE Staff/Lead Product Designer, Design System Finland 21 Aug eBay Principal Designer - Design Systems USA 21 Aug Figma Product Designer, AI Models USA remote 21 Aug Harvey Product Designer, Design Systems USA 21 Aug Your agent then keeps the ones that match your CV and tells you what you are missing per role. It reads the requirements the company wrote and not the job title. 2. “Only the remote ones that ask for AI skills please” Across the whole board 32 roles are remote and name AI or agentic skills in the posting. Those are the ones I would read first. 3. “Compare the Netflix and the General Motors role for me. Which one is closer to what I have done?” Two postings side by side with your CV as the yardstick. 4. “Put the eight best matches in a table with company and title and link and one line on why it fits. Save it as shortlist.md” Now you have one working file instead of twelve open tabs. Tell it to strike the row once you have applied. 5. “Go through shortlist.md and tell me which of these roles are still open” Closed postings drop off the board so this is a real check and not a guess. Run it before you spend an evening on an application for a role that filled two weeks ago. I want a number for the salary talk Three prompts so you name a figure that came from postings and not from a feeling. 6. “What do postings pay for a Staff level Design System role?” 46 postings state a range themselves. The median sits between 162,600 and 220,000 USD and the highest range on the board tops out at 710,000. Almost all of those postings are US roles because pay transparency laws require the number there so do not carry them into another country. 7. “Which US roles ask for design tokens and what do they pay?” 17 US postings name design tokens. Eleven of them state a range and four of those top out above 200,000 USD. The highest is the Netflix Systems Designer role in Design Foundations at 260,000 to 400,000. 8. “This posting states no salary. What do comparable roles on the board pay?” You get the range from the postings that do state one plus which level and country they came from. That is a reference point and not their budget. Say the number first anyway. I want to know what to learn next Four prompts for the months when you are not applying and want to be ready when you are. 9. “Which skills come up in most postings that my CV does not mention?” Run this when you are not applying yet. It tells you what to learn next instead of guessing. 93 of the 135 postings we hold the full text for ask for AI or agentic skills. 10. “Read the Netflix posting. Which requirements do I not have yet and where do I learn them?” The server does not stop at the gap. find_learning takes the missing skill and helps you find where to learn it. It names the recorded conference session from the Into Design Systems AI Conference that covers it. Ask about MCP and you get Diana Wolosin , Netflix (ex Indeed) on machine-readable design systems for MCP and LLMs. Ask about agentic design systems and you get Romina Kavcic on the five agentic flows. 11. “Which roles do not ask for AI skills at all?” 48 of the described postings ask for none. Useful if you are still building that muscle and want something you can start on Monday. 12. “Which words do these postings use for the work I already do?” Vocabulary research and nothing else. You still write your own CV but you write it in the words the market uses. I want to walk into the interview prepared Four prompts that turn their own posting into your prep sheet. 13. “Read this posting and tell me the three things they care about most and what I should have ready as evidence” My prep prompt. You get their own wording back plus the questions worth preparing for. 14. “What does this posting not ask for?” Stops you preparing three days for a topic nobody will bring up. 15. “Give me three questions to ask them at the end. Base them on their own posting” Questions that come out of their requirements land differently than the ones everybody asks. 16. “Which companies have more than three roles open?” General Motors has 5 and Netflix has 4. Coinbase and ESET and Yassir have 3 each. Several roles open at once usually means a team is being built. Worth a direct message. I want to know where the roles are Four prompts before you plan a move or a timezone or a year of applications. 17. “Where do most Design System roles sit right now?” USA has 119 and the United Kingdom 16 and Germany 14. Canada and France have 12 each. Useful if you are weighing a move or a timezone. 18. “How many of the German roles can be done remotely?” One of the 14. Ask that before you spend a year applying from a country you do not want to move to. 19. “How concentrated is the board? How many companies are hiring and how many have more than one role?” 190 companies are hiring right now and 27 of them have two or more roles open. 20. “Are there contract roles?” Seven right now. get_job carries the employment type so you can sort permanent from contract before you read anything. I am the one hiring Three prompts for the other side of the table. 21. “Compare our job description against the open Design System postings and tell me what other companies name that we leave out” You get back what the other postings name and your description leaves out. 22. “What do other companies call this role?” 88 of the open postings carry Design System Designer in the title and 94 carry Product Designer and 23 carry Design System Engineer. 98 say Staff or Senior. Name the role the way the people you want are searching. 23. “Who are we competing with for these people right now?” Every company with an open role in your corner of the board plus how many they have open. That is your candidate’s other tab. Step 3: let it check the board every morning A cron job is your Mac running something on a schedule without you. You never have to write one. You describe what should happen and when and Claude Code sets it up. The daily check Save your CV as cv.md in a folder. Mine is ~/jobs . Start Claude Code in that folder and paste this. 24. “Set up a job check that runs every weekday at 8 in the morning. Read cv.md in this folder. Ask the ids-jobs server for the roles posted in the last seven days that can be done remotely and keep the ones that fit my CV. Write them into today.md with one line per role: company and title and why it fits. If nothing fits write nothing new. It has to run on its own without asking me anything because I am not at the machine at 8. Put it in my crontab and run it once now so I can see that it works.” Claude writes the script and sets the schedule and shows you the first result. Here is what came back for me: SAP Senior UX Designer - Design Systems Microsoft Principal Product Designer, Design Systems Netflix Systems Designer, Design Foundations Clio Staff Product Designer, Design Systems Babylist Staff Product Designer, AI Builder Two things to know before you run it. The one click you have to give: Claude asks before it edits your crontab. Say yes and it is done. Full Disk Access: on macOS your terminal needs it under System Settings then Privacy and Security. Without it the 8 o’clock run cannot read your CV. Four more worth scheduling The daily check is one job. These four run next to it. 25. “Same thing but once a week. Monday at 9. Everything from the last seven days grouped by country and put the remote ones first” The daily one is for an active search. This is the version you keep running when you are not looking. It takes two minutes to read on Monday. 26. “Watch Figma and Netflix and Atlassian for me. Check every morning and only write something into watch.md when one of them posts a new Design System role” For the three companies you would leave for. Silence most days is the point. 27. “On the first of every month ask for the hiring numbers and append them to market.md with the date. Open roles and remote share and AI share and the salary range” After four months you have your own trend line. The board only tells you today and the file tells you the direction. 28. “Send the result to name@example.com instead of writing a file” Add that sentence to any of the prompts above and it lands in your inbox. Checking and stopping it You never open crontab yourself. You ask. 29. “Show me what you scheduled and when it runs next” 30. “Stop the daily job check but leave the Monday one running” You never touch crontab yourself. You say what you want and Claude edits it. What it does not do It does not apply for you: every role links to the employer’s own page and the server never sends anything on your behalf. It should not write your cover letter: a letter that came out of a model reads like one. Use this to work out what the role wants and then write it yourself. It only knows Design System and AI design roles: nothing else is on the board. Try it claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp Setup page with all clients: jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp-guide . The board itself lives at jobs.intodesignsystems.com . A longer version of this walkthrough lives on our blog. It adds what to put in cv.md so the matching actually works plus a troubleshooting table for the things that go wrong: read it on intodesignsystems.com . Good luck! You got this! If you get stuck or you have an idea for a tool the server should have then write me on LinkedIn . Sil Bormüller Founder @ Into Design Systems P.S. Missing the AI skills these roles ask for? Level up. The Into Design Systems AI conference has hands-on talks on AI workflows and Claude Code and Cursor and Design System automation from industry experts. visualFeast.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! Leave a comment And please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net . Previously: OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. graphicDesign.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
graphicDesign.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. graphicDesign.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
graphicDesign.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. graphicDesign.title: Step by step: How to find Design System + AI jobs faster with Claude Code and MCP
graphicDesign.description: I gave our Design System job board an MCP server. Your AI agent can read the whole job board now. (What is an MCP? MCP is the standard that lets an agent call a tool instead of scraping a web page) Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Why? Good roles go early. By the time you have scrolled the job board and opened twelve tabs and read the postings properly the pile on the recruiter’s desk is deep. There are 225 open Design System roles on the board right now. Every one of them is checked by hand and closed postings drop out. Nobody reads 225 postings. You read four and apply to two. Your agent works through all of them. It runs at https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp It needs no key and no account and it can only read Below are the 30 prompts I run against it The last ones hand the whole job over to a cron job that checks the board every morning for you What is inside One line to connect the server. Everything after it is a prompt. 23 prompts for finding roles and reading salary bands and closing skill gaps and preparing for the interview. 7 prompts that hand the search to a cron job so your Mac checks the board while you sleep. The five tools and what each one answers. Step 1: connect it One line in your terminal (1 min) Paste this in Claude Code: claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp The -s user part registers it for every folder. Leave it out and the server only exists in the folder you happened to be in. Then restart Claude Code once because tools load when a session starts. Quit it with /exit and start it again and ask “which tools do you have from ids-jobs?” No terminal at all? Claude Desktop and claude.ai do it in the interface: Settings then Connectors then Add custom connector. Paste the URL and start a new chat. Cursor and every other MCP client work too. The setup page has the config for each of them. Step 2: the prompts Put your CV in the folder you start Claude Code in or simply describe your skills. Then use these. Every number under a prompt is what the board answered on 21 August 2026. I want the roles that are worth my time Five prompts that cut 225 postings down to the handful you would actually take. 1. “Which Design System roles were posted in the last two weeks? Optional: Which of them fit my CV?” The one I use most. 57 roles came in over the last fourteen days. Here are the five newest: Malt Head of Experience Systems & AI France / Germany 21 Aug ICEYE Staff/Lead Product Designer, Design System Finland 21 Aug eBay Principal Designer - Design Systems USA 21 Aug Figma Product Designer, AI Models USA remote 21 Aug Harvey Product Designer, Design Systems USA 21 Aug Your agent then keeps the ones that match your CV and tells you what you are missing per role. It reads the requirements the company wrote and not the job title. 2. “Only the remote ones that ask for AI skills please” Across the whole board 32 roles are remote and name AI or agentic skills in the posting. Those are the ones I would read first. 3. “Compare the Netflix and the General Motors role for me. Which one is closer to what I have done?” Two postings side by side with your CV as the yardstick. 4. “Put the eight best matches in a table with company and title and link and one line on why it fits. Save it as shortlist.md” Now you have one working file instead of twelve open tabs. Tell it to strike the row once you have applied. 5. “Go through shortlist.md and tell me which of these roles are still open” Closed postings drop off the board so this is a real check and not a guess. Run it before you spend an evening on an application for a role that filled two weeks ago. I want a number for the salary talk Three prompts so you name a figure that came from postings and not from a feeling. 6. “What do postings pay for a Staff level Design System role?” 46 postings state a range themselves. The median sits between 162,600 and 220,000 USD and the highest range on the board tops out at 710,000. Almost all of those postings are US roles because pay transparency laws require the number there so do not carry them into another country. 7. “Which US roles ask for design tokens and what do they pay?” 17 US postings name design tokens. Eleven of them state a range and four of those top out above 200,000 USD. The highest is the Netflix Systems Designer role in Design Foundations at 260,000 to 400,000. 8. “This posting states no salary. What do comparable roles on the board pay?” You get the range from the postings that do state one plus which level and country they came from. That is a reference point and not their budget. Say the number first anyway. I want to know what to learn next Four prompts for the months when you are not applying and want to be ready when you are. 9. “Which skills come up in most postings that my CV does not mention?” Run this when you are not applying yet. It tells you what to learn next instead of guessing. 93 of the 135 postings we hold the full text for ask for AI or agentic skills. 10. “Read the Netflix posting. Which requirements do I not have yet and where do I learn them?” The server does not stop at the gap. find_learning takes the missing skill and helps you find where to learn it. It names the recorded conference session from the Into Design Systems AI Conference that covers it. Ask about MCP and you get Diana Wolosin , Netflix (ex Indeed) on machine-readable design systems for MCP and LLMs. Ask about agentic design systems and you get Romina Kavcic on the five agentic flows. 11. “Which roles do not ask for AI skills at all?” 48 of the described postings ask for none. Useful if you are still building that muscle and want something you can start on Monday. 12. “Which words do these postings use for the work I already do?” Vocabulary research and nothing else. You still write your own CV but you write it in the words the market uses. I want to walk into the interview prepared Four prompts that turn their own posting into your prep sheet. 13. “Read this posting and tell me the three things they care about most and what I should have ready as evidence” My prep prompt. You get their own wording back plus the questions worth preparing for. 14. “What does this posting not ask for?” Stops you preparing three days for a topic nobody will bring up. 15. “Give me three questions to ask them at the end. Base them on their own posting” Questions that come out of their requirements land differently than the ones everybody asks. 16. “Which companies have more than three roles open?” General Motors has 5 and Netflix has 4. Coinbase and ESET and Yassir have 3 each. Several roles open at once usually means a team is being built. Worth a direct message. I want to know where the roles are Four prompts before you plan a move or a timezone or a year of applications. 17. “Where do most Design System roles sit right now?” USA has 119 and the United Kingdom 16 and Germany 14. Canada and France have 12 each. Useful if you are weighing a move or a timezone. 18. “How many of the German roles can be done remotely?” One of the 14. Ask that before you spend a year applying from a country you do not want to move to. 19. “How concentrated is the board? How many companies are hiring and how many have more than one role?” 190 companies are hiring right now and 27 of them have two or more roles open. 20. “Are there contract roles?” Seven right now. get_job carries the employment type so you can sort permanent from contract before you read anything. I am the one hiring Three prompts for the other side of the table. 21. “Compare our job description against the open Design System postings and tell me what other companies name that we leave out” You get back what the other postings name and your description leaves out. 22. “What do other companies call this role?” 88 of the open postings carry Design System Designer in the title and 94 carry Product Designer and 23 carry Design System Engineer. 98 say Staff or Senior. Name the role the way the people you want are searching. 23. “Who are we competing with for these people right now?” Every company with an open role in your corner of the board plus how many they have open. That is your candidate’s other tab. Step 3: let it check the board every morning A cron job is your Mac running something on a schedule without you. You never have to write one. You describe what should happen and when and Claude Code sets it up. The daily check Save your CV as cv.md in a folder. Mine is ~/jobs . Start Claude Code in that folder and paste this. 24. “Set up a job check that runs every weekday at 8 in the morning. Read cv.md in this folder. Ask the ids-jobs server for the roles posted in the last seven days that can be done remotely and keep the ones that fit my CV. Write them into today.md with one line per role: company and title and why it fits. If nothing fits write nothing new. It has to run on its own without asking me anything because I am not at the machine at 8. Put it in my crontab and run it once now so I can see that it works.” Claude writes the script and sets the schedule and shows you the first result. Here is what came back for me: SAP Senior UX Designer - Design Systems Microsoft Principal Product Designer, Design Systems Netflix Systems Designer, Design Foundations Clio Staff Product Designer, Design Systems Babylist Staff Product Designer, AI Builder Two things to know before you run it. The one click you have to give: Claude asks before it edits your crontab. Say yes and it is done. Full Disk Access: on macOS your terminal needs it under System Settings then Privacy and Security. Without it the 8 o’clock run cannot read your CV. Four more worth scheduling The daily check is one job. These four run next to it. 25. “Same thing but once a week. Monday at 9. Everything from the last seven days grouped by country and put the remote ones first” The daily one is for an active search. This is the version you keep running when you are not looking. It takes two minutes to read on Monday. 26. “Watch Figma and Netflix and Atlassian for me. Check every morning and only write something into watch.md when one of them posts a new Design System role” For the three companies you would leave for. Silence most days is the point. 27. “On the first of every month ask for the hiring numbers and append them to market.md with the date. Open roles and remote share and AI share and the salary range” After four months you have your own trend line. The board only tells you today and the file tells you the direction. 28. “Send the result to name@example.com instead of writing a file” Add that sentence to any of the prompts above and it lands in your inbox. Checking and stopping it You never open crontab yourself. You ask. 29. “Show me what you scheduled and when it runs next” 30. “Stop the daily job check but leave the Monday one running” You never touch crontab yourself. You say what you want and Claude edits it. What it does not do It does not apply for you: every role links to the employer’s own page and the server never sends anything on your behalf. It should not write your cover letter: a letter that came out of a model reads like one. Use this to work out what the role wants and then write it yourself. It only knows Design System and AI design roles: nothing else is on the board. Try it claude mcp add -s user --transport http ids-jobs https://jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp Setup page with all clients: jobs.intodesignsystems.com/mcp-guide . The board itself lives at jobs.intodesignsystems.com . A longer version of this walkthrough lives on our blog. It adds what to put in cv.md so the matching actually works plus a troubleshooting table for the things that go wrong: read it on intodesignsystems.com . Good luck! You got this! If you get stuck or you have an idea for a tool the server should have then write me on LinkedIn . Sil Bormüller Founder @ Into Design Systems P.S. Missing the AI skills these roles ask for? Level up. The Into Design Systems AI conference has hands-on talks on AI workflows and Claude Code and Cursor and Design System automation from industry experts. O Senado dos EUA criou um grupo bipartidário para ouvir criadores de conteúdo e discutir políticas para o setor. Uma das primeiras pautas é a proteção da imagem e da voz contra réplicas feitas por IA sem autorização. A União Europeia quer mexer não só na idade, mas no design das redes para crianças. wild.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
wild.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. People Joss Fong, video journalist on science and tech, formerly of Vox, now co-founder of Howtown: joss-fong.com Áron Filkey, art director and visual artist working across photo, motion, and set design: aronfilkey.com Simon Caspersen, co-founder of Space10 and ArtRebels. Torbjörn Lööf, then-CEO of IKEA when Space10 was founded. ArtRebels, the Danish design collective behind Space10’s original concept: artrebels.com Further reading Collected Consciousness , DOC: doc.cc/articles/consciousness Efficiency over Craftsmanship , UX Collective: uxdesign.cc/efficiency-over-craftsmanship
